newsitem.title: USA: Clinton ponders line-item veto, makes no decisions.
newsitem.headline: Clinton ponders line-item veto, makes no decisions.

text.p: President Bill Clinton and his advisers on Thursday debated using his new powers to strip a handful of tax and spending items from the balanced-budget agreement but made no decisions, a White House official said.

Clinton, who this week signed legislation that aims to balance the U.S. federal budget by the year 2002 while cutting taxes by $95 billion, has until midnight on Monday to use the so-called line-item veto to strike down parts of that law.

At a news conference on Wednesday, the president said he expected to use the veto for the first time on the budget pact despite the legal challenges expected to be filed against the veto power, which came into effect at the start of the year.

The White House official, who asked not to be identified, said Clinton asked his advisers at a meeting late on Thursday for more information and said deliberations would continue on Friday and into the weekend.
The official said the White House is weighing items in both the tax and the spending bills that together make up the balanced-budget legislation.
The administration was previously thought to be focusing on 79 items identified in the tax bill as benefiting narrow groups and therefore considered ripe targets for the veto.
One official said the White House would prefer to unveil a decision on Saturday, in Clinton's weekly radio address, but said the president may wait until Monday to make a decision.
In pondering his first use of the line-item veto, Clinton, a Democrat, faces both political and legal obstacles.

On the one hand, he has said he would not use the veto to strike down anything that he and the Republicans who control both houses of Congress explicitly agreed to in the tortuous negotiations over balancing the budget.
On the other, aides said that he is factoring the expected court challenges into his thinking on what to target.

The 1996 law has already survived one legal challenge this year. The Supreme Court in June ruled that six members of Congress who filed suit against the law did not have the right to contest the veto because it had not yet been exercised.
The law, passed by Congress last year, was initially touted as a way of reducing the deficit by stripping out special-interest items in the budget.

Long sought by presidents and a key part of the Republican agenda when the party won control of Congress in 1994, the law allows a president to cancel items involving appropriations bills, certain tax breaks and new or expanded entitlements.
Like other presidential vetoes, Congress can override the action by mustering a two-thirds majority in both the House and Senate.
